**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geology 2 (0755), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2024. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, ONE from each section. All questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the value of clear sketches, even when not specifically demanded by the wording of the question, and of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Question 4(c) : FAIT LOCAL à faire relire par un géologue. Le corrigé cite le bassin de Rio del Rey, le bassin de Douala et le bassin de Kribi-Campo (souvent regroupés en « bassin de Douala/Kribi-Campo » ou « bassin de Douala-Kribi/Campo ») comme bassins sédimentaires côtiers du Cameroun ; aucun âge ni épaisseur précis n'est donné (seulement « Crétacé à Tertiaire »), car la nomenclature varie selon les auteurs.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Give an account of the characteristics of arenaceous rocks.

(12 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Arenaceous rocks** (the sandstones and their relatives) are **clastic sedimentary rocks made mainly of sand-size grains (0.0625 to 2 mm)**, cemented together. They form about a quarter of all sedimentary rocks. Their characteristics are as follows.

1. **Texture.** The grains are **fragments of pre-existing rocks and minerals** that were transported and deposited, so the rock has a **fragmental (clastic) texture**, with a visible, gritty sand-size grain that is **often rounded** (rounding and sorting increase with the distance of transport). The grains may be **well sorted** (of one size, as in dune and beach sands) or **poorly sorted** (as in river and flood deposits). The rock may be **fine, medium or coarse-grained**.
2. **Composition.** **Quartz** is by far the most abundant grain because it is hard and chemically stable; there may also be **feldspar, mica, rock fragments (lithic grains), and heavy minerals** such as zircon, tourmaline and magnetite. Fossils are usually rare.
3. **Matrix and cement.** The spaces between the grains may contain a fine-grained **matrix** (clay and silt) and are bound by **cement**, deposited from water that circulates through the rock: **silica (quartz), calcite, iron oxide (haematite, limonite) or clay**. The type of cement determines the **hardness, colour and resistance** of the rock.
4. **Colour.** Usually pale (white, grey, yellow), **red or brown** when the grains are coated by **iron oxide**, green when glauconite is present.
5. **Porosity and permeability.** Because of the packing of the grains, sandstones are **porous (often 10 to 30 %) and permeable**: they make good **aquifers** and, with an impermeable seal, **oil and gas reservoirs**.
6. **Sedimentary structures.** **Bedding and lamination**, **cross-bedding** (dunes, rivers), **ripple marks**, **graded bedding** (turbidites), channel structures, sole markings and, in some cases, mud cracks and burrows.
7. **Main types (classification by composition).**
   - **Quartz arenite (orthoquartzite)**: more than 90 to 95 % quartz, well sorted and well rounded, a **mature** sandstone from beaches, deserts and shallow seas; very hard.
   - **Arkose**: contains a high proportion of feldspar (about 25 % or more), angular grains, usually pink or red; it is derived rapidly from a granitic source with little weathering and short transport (an **immature** sandstone).
   - **Greywacke (lithic wacke)**: dark, **poorly sorted**, with angular quartz and rock fragments in an abundant clay matrix (more than about 15 %); typical of deep-water turbidity-current deposits.
   - **Lithic arenite (litharenite)**: contains many rock fragments.
8. **Environments of deposition.** Rivers, deltas, beaches and shallow seas, **desert dunes** and turbidity currents in deep water.
9. **Economic uses.** Building stone and aggregate, grindstone, **glass sand (silica sand)**, **aquifers** and petroleum **reservoirs**, and sources of heavy minerals (placer deposits, tin and gold).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Briefly discuss the weathering processes most likely to affect rocks in the following areas:

(i) Deserts;

(ii) Tropical regions.

(10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Weathering** is the breakdown of rocks in place at or near the surface, by **physical (mechanical)**, **chemical** and **biological** processes. The dominant process depends on the climate.

**(i) Deserts (hot and dry: little water, very large daily range of temperature).** **Physical weathering dominates.**

- **Thermal expansion and contraction (insolation weathering):** the rock surface is heated strongly by day and cools quickly at night. The minerals expand and contract by different amounts, which produces stress that makes the rock **crack and peel off in sheets or flakes (exfoliation)** or split into grains (**granular disintegration**).
- **Salt crystallisation (salt weathering):** water that is drawn to the surface by evaporation leaves salt crystals in pores and cracks; as they grow and as they expand on heating, they **force the grains apart** and the rock crumbles (a big effect near the sea and in salt pans).
- **Frost action** in cold deserts and mountain areas (freeze-thaw), and **pressure release (unloading)** of rocks such as granite.
- **Chemical weathering is slow and weak** because of the lack of water: some oxidation of iron minerals, and the formation of a dark **desert varnish** on the rock surface by dew. Physical weathering produces angular fragments and sand, which the wind and flash floods transport.

**(ii) Tropical regions (hot and humid: high rainfall, high temperature, dense vegetation).** **Chemical weathering dominates**, and is **fast and deep**, because the speed of chemical reactions increases with temperature and water.

- **Hydrolysis:** feldspars and other silicates react with slightly acidic rain water and are changed into **clay minerals (kaolinite)**, with silica and ions removed in solution; the residue may be enriched in aluminium (**bauxite**) and iron to form **laterite** (a red, iron-rich soil).
- **Oxidation:** iron-bearing minerals react with oxygen to give **red and brown iron oxides** (haematite, goethite), which colour tropical soils.
- **Solution and carbonation:** water containing carbon dioxide dissolves **limestone** (karst, caves and sinkholes).
- **Hydration** of some minerals (anhydrite to gypsum), and **organic (biological) weathering:** acids from decaying plants (humic acids), **roots** that wedge in joints, bacteria and burrowing animals.
- Joints are attacked and a **deep weathering profile** (regolith) may reach tens of metres; blocks of granite are rounded by **spheroidal weathering (onion-skin weathering)**, leaving corestones.

So the weathering in the **desert is mainly physical** and produces **angular debris**, while in the **tropics it is mainly chemical** and produces **clay, laterite and deep soils**.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) State the coastal sedimentary basins in Cameroon.

(3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The coastal sedimentary basins of Cameroon, which lie along the Gulf of Guinea, are:

1. **The Rio del Rey Basin**, in the south-west, in the Bakassi and Southern Cameroons area (an oil-producing delta basin that continues offshore).
2. **The Douala Basin** (the Douala sub-basin of the Douala/Kribi-Campo Basin), around Douala.
3. **The Kribi-Campo Basin** (the Kribi-Campo sub-basin), in the south, near Kribi and Campo.

(The Douala and Kribi-Campo basins are sometimes treated together as one **Douala/Kribi-Campo Basin**. They contain mostly Cretaceous to Tertiary sedimentary rocks.)
